title: Contains Duplicate
description: You're given an array of numbers, nums. Check if any number shows up more than once anywhere in the array. If any number repeats, return true. If every number is completely different from every other number, return false.

examples.explanation: The number 1 shows up twice.
Every number in the array is unique.

hints: Use a HashSet to keep track of numbers you've already seen.
The moment you try to add a number that's already in the set, you can immediately return true.
followUp: Can you solve it without extra space using sorting?

testCases.note: Standard case with an obvious duplicate.
All values are distinct.
Edge case: only one element, so there's nothing to duplicate.
Edge case: the same number is repeated many times.
Edge case: negative numbers can be duplicates too.

title: Two Sum
description: You're given a list of numbers, nums, and a target number. Find the two numbers in the list that add up exactly to target, and return their positions (indices). You can assume there's always exactly one correct pair, and you can't use the same element twice.
hints: Store each number you've seen, along with its index, in a HashMap.
For every number, check whether (target - number) already exists in your HashMap.
followUp: What if the array is sorted?

testCases.note: Standard example.
Answer is not at the start of the array.
Edge case: the two matching numbers are identical.
Edge case: negative numbers are involved.
Edge case: the smallest possible array length.

title: Valid Anagram
description: You're given two strings, s and t. Check whether t is an anagram of s — meaning t is made from exactly the same letters as s, used the exact same number of times, just arranged differently. For example, 'listen' and 'silent' are anagrams because they share the exact same letters.

examples.explanation: Both strings use the exact same letters the exact same number of times.
The letters used in each string are different.

constraints: s and t consist of lowercase English letters.
hints: Count how often each character appears using a HashMap.
Compare the two frequency counts, or subtract one from the other and check that everything cancels out to zero.
relatedProblems: Find All Anagrams in a String
followUp: What if inputs contain Unicode characters?

testCases.note: Standard matching case.
Completely different letters.
Edge case: smallest possible input, a single matching letter.
Edge case: strings of different lengths can never be anagrams.
Edge case: repeated letters, still matches when counted correctly.

title: Design HashMap
description: Build your own HashMap, without using any programming language's built-in hash table. You need three operations: put(key, value) to insert or update a key-value pair, get(key) to look up a value (returning -1 if the key was never inserted), and remove(key) to delete a key-value pair if it exists.

examples.input: put(1,1), put(2,2), get(1), get(3), put(2,1), get(2), remove(2), get(2)
examples.explanation: A typical sequence of insert, lookup, update, and remove operations.
After removing a key, looking it up again returns -1.

constraints: At most 10^4 calls to put, get, and remove.
hints: Use an array where each slot holds a small list of key-value pairs (this is called chaining).
A simple hash function like key % tableSize works well to pick which slot to use.
followUp: How would you handle resizing?

testCases.note: Basic insert and lookup.
Edge case: looking up a key that was never inserted.
Edge case: putting the same key twice should update its value.
Edge case: removing a key makes future lookups return -1.
Edge case: removing a key that was never inserted shouldn't cause any errors.

title: Design HashSet
description: Build your own HashSet, without using any built-in set library. You need three operations: add(key) to insert a value if it's not already there, contains(key) to check whether a value exists, and remove(key) to delete a value if it exists.

examples.input: add(1), add(2), contains(1), contains(3), add(2), contains(2), remove(2), contains(2)
examples.explanation: A typical sequence of add, contains, and remove operations.
After removing a value, checking for it again returns false.

constraints: At most 10^4 calls to add, remove, and contains.
hints: Use an array of buckets, where each bucket holds a small list of values.
Use a simple modulo operation as your hash function to decide which bucket a value goes into.
followUp: Compare your design with Java's HashSet implementation.

testCases.note: Basic add and lookup.
Edge case: checking a value that was never added.
Edge case: adding the same value twice shouldn't cause problems.
Edge case: removing a value makes contains() return false afterward.
Edge case: removing a value that was never added shouldn't cause any errors.

title: Jewels and Stones
description: You're given two strings: jewels, which lists which letter types count as jewels, and stones, which represents the stones you actually own. Count how many of your stones are jewels. Letters are case-sensitive, so 'a' and 'A' are treated as completely different types.

examples.explanation: The stones 'a', 'A', and 'A' are all jewels.
Since letters are case-sensitive, 'Z' does not match 'z'.

hints: Put every character from jewels into a HashSet first.
Then count how many characters in stones exist in that HashSet.
followUp: What if the input is a stream?

testCases.note: Standard example with mixed matches.
Case sensitivity means no matches.
Edge case: smallest possible input, exactly one matching stone.
Edge case: the same jewel letter repeats many times in stones.
Edge case: none of the stones are jewels at all.

title: Maximum Number of Balloons
description: You're given a string, text. Figure out how many times you can spell out the word 'balloon' using only the letters available in text (each letter in text can only be used once). Spelling 'balloon' requires: one 'b', one 'a', two 'l's, two 'o's, and one 'n'.

examples.explanation: There are just enough letters to spell 'balloon' exactly once.
There are enough letters to spell 'balloon' twice.

constraints: text consists of lower case English letters only.
hints: Count how many times each of b, a, l, o, and n appears in text.
Remember that l and o are each needed twice per 'balloon', so divide those two counts by 2.
relatedProblems: Find All Anagrams in a String
followUp: Can you generalize for any target word?

testCases.note: Exactly enough letters for one balloon.
Enough letters for two balloons.
Edge case: the input is exactly the word itself.
Edge case: almost none of the required letters are present.
Edge case: has b, a, and l but is completely missing 'o' and 'n', so zero balloons can be formed.

title: Word Pattern
description: You're given a short pattern (like 'abba') and a sentence s made of space-separated words. Check if the words in s follow the exact same pattern as the letters. This means each letter in the pattern must always correspond to the exact same word, and no two different letters can correspond to the same word (a strict one-to-one relationship in both directions).

examples.explanation: 'a' consistently maps to 'dog' and 'b' consistently maps to 'cat'.
The last word 'fish' should have matched 'dog' (since the first and last letters are both 'a'), but it doesn't.

constraints: s contains only lowercase English words separated by a single space.
hints: Use two HashMaps: one mapping pattern-letter to word, and one mapping word to pattern-letter.
At every position, check that both mappings agree — if either one is broken, return false.
followUp: What about Word Pattern II?

testCases.note: Consistent mapping in both directions.
The pattern breaks at the last word.
Edge case: pattern says all letters are the same, but the words differ.
Edge case: two different pattern letters ('a' and 'b') would both map to the same word, breaking the one-to-one rule.
Edge case: smallest possible input, a single letter mapped to a single word.

title: Isomorphic Strings
description: You're given two strings, s and t, of the same length. Check whether they are 'isomorphic' — meaning you could replace every character in s with some other character to get exactly t, following a strict one-to-one rule (no two different characters in s can map to the same character, and each character always maps to exactly one character). For example, 'egg' and 'add' are isomorphic because every 'e' becomes 'a' and every 'g' becomes 'd'. But 'foo' and 'bar' are not, because the letter 'o' would need to become both 'a' and 'r', which breaks the rule.

examples.explanation: 'e' consistently maps to 'a' and 'g' consistently maps to 'd'.
'o' would need to map to both 'a' and 'r', which isn't allowed.

hints: Use two HashMaps: one mapping s-character to t-character, and one mapping t-character to s-character.
Check both maps agree at every single position as you scan through the strings.
followUp: Can you solve using only one map?

testCases.note: Consistent character mapping.
One character would need two different mappings.
A slightly longer example with a valid consistent mapping.
Edge case: two different source characters ('a' and 'b') would both need to map to 'a', breaking the one-to-one rule.
Edge case: smallest possible input, a single matching character.

title: Ransom Note
description: You're given two strings: ransomNote and magazine. Check whether you can build ransomNote by using individual letters from magazine, where each letter in magazine can only be used once.

examples.explanation: The letter 'a' isn't available anywhere in magazine.
magazine has two 'a's available, which is exactly enough.

hints: Count how many times each letter appears in magazine.
Go through ransomNote and check that magazine has enough of every needed letter.
followUp: What if each letter can only be used once?

testCases.note: Needed letter isn't available at all.
Exactly enough copies available.
Edge case: not quite enough copies of a needed letter.
Edge case: smallest possible input, exact single-letter match.
Edge case: an exact match using every single letter available.

title: Intersection of Two Arrays
description: You're given two arrays of numbers, nums1 and nums2. Find all the numbers that appear in both arrays, and return them with no duplicates in your answer (even if a number repeats several times in either array).

examples.explanation: 2 is the only number common to both arrays, and it appears once in the answer.
Both 4 and 9 appear in both arrays.

hints: Put all of nums1's numbers into a HashSet first.
Then check each number in nums2 against that HashSet to build your answer.
followUp: What if the given array is already sorted?

testCases.note: Standard example with a repeated common number.
Multiple common numbers, each returned once.
Edge case: the two arrays have nothing in common.
Edge case: heavy duplicates on both sides still collapse to a single answer.
Edge case: smallest possible arrays, both matching.

title: Group Anagrams
description: You're given a list of strings. Group together all the strings that are anagrams of each other, and return the groups in any order.

examples.explanation: Strings sharing the same sorted letters get grouped together.
A single empty string simply forms its own group.

hints: Sort each string's letters to create a shared 'signature' key.
Use a HashMap where the key is the signature and the value is a list of the original strings.
relatedProblems: Find All Anagrams in a String
followUp: Can you use character frequency as the key instead of sorting?

testCases.note: Standard multi-group example.
Edge case: a single empty string is allowed by the constraints.
Edge case: a single one-letter string with no group to join.
Edge case: one matching pair plus one string that stands alone.
Edge case: multiple empty strings all belong to the same group.

title: Top K Frequent Elements
description: You're given an array of numbers and a number k. Return the k numbers that appear most often in the array, in any order. It's guaranteed there's exactly one correct set of answers.

examples.explanation: 1 appears 3 times and 2 appears 2 times — the two most frequent numbers.
There's only one number, so it's automatically the most frequent.

constraints: k is in the range [1, number of unique elements]
hints: First, count how often each number appears using a HashMap.
Then use a min-heap of size k, or try bucket sort by frequency for an even faster solution.
relatedProblems: Kth Largest Element in an Array
followUp: Can you solve it in O(n) time using bucket sort?

testCases.note: Standard case with clear frequency ranking.
Edge case: smallest possible input, one element.
Edge case: k equals the total number of unique elements.
Edge case: only one unique number in the whole array.
Edge case: strictly one number is clearly the most frequent.

title: Longest Consecutive Sequence
description: You're given an unsorted array of numbers. Find the length of the longest run of consecutive numbers that all appear somewhere in the array (for example, [1,2,3,4] is a run of length 4, even if they're scattered around in the original array).

examples.explanation: The numbers 1, 2, 3, 4 form the longest consecutive run.
The numbers 0 through 8 form one long consecutive run.

hints: Put all the numbers into a HashSet for instant lookups.
Only start counting a new sequence from a number if (number - 1) is not already in the set.
followUp: What if the array is already sorted?

testCases.note: Standard case with a clear consecutive run.
A longer run that also includes a duplicate number.
Edge case: an empty array is allowed by the constraints.
Edge case: duplicate values shouldn't affect the sequence length.
Edge case: a single-element array is its own run of length 1.

title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
description: You're given a string. Find the length of the longest continuous chunk of it that has no repeated characters at all.

examples.explanation: "abc" is the longest chunk with no repeated characters.
Any window bigger than a single 'b' would contain a repeat.

constraints: s consists of English letters, digits, symbols and spaces.
hints: Maintain a sliding window using a HashSet of currently 'active' characters.
When you find a duplicate, move the left pointer forward until that duplicate is removed from the window.

youtubeVideos.title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters - NeetCode

relatedProblems: Longest Substring with At Most Two Distinct Characters
followUp: Can you use a HashMap storing indices to optimize the left pointer movement?

testCases.note: Standard case with a repeating pattern.
Every character in the string is the same.
Edge case: an empty string is allowed by the constraints.
Edge case: every character is already unique.
Edge case: a repeat in the middle tests correct window shrinking.

title: 4Sum II
description: You're given four separate arrays of numbers, all the same length. Count how many combinations you can make — picking exactly one number from each array — that add up to exactly zero.

examples.explanation: There are exactly two combinations, one from each array, that add up to zero.
The only possible combination (0+0+0+0) sums to zero.

hints: Compute every sum of (nums1[i] + nums2[j]) and store how often each sum occurs in a HashMap.
For every sum of (nums3[k] + nums4[l]), check if the negative of that sum exists in your HashMap.
followUp: How would you extend this to k arrays?

testCases.note: Standard case with two valid combinations.
Edge case: smallest possible arrays (n=1), all zeros.
Edge case: n=1 with a single valid zero-sum combination.
Edge case: no combination at all sums to zero.
Edge case: every possible combination sums to zero, producing the maximum count for n=2.

title: Find All Anagrams in a String
description: You're given two strings, s and p. Find every starting position in s where a chunk of the same length as p is an anagram of p (uses the exact same letters, just rearranged).

examples.explanation: The chunk "cba" at index 0 and "bac" at index 6 are both anagrams of "abc".
Every 2-character chunk starting at these indices is an anagram of "ab".

constraints: s and p consist of lowercase English letters.
hints: Use a fixed-size sliding window equal to the length of p.
Compare character frequency counts inside the window against the frequency counts of p.

youtubeVideos.title: Find All Anagrams in a String - NeetCode

followUp: Can you use a difference counter to avoid comparing two maps?

testCases.note: Standard example with two matches.
Overlapping matches across the string.
Edge case: p is longer than s, so no match is possible.
Edge case: smallest possible matching input.
Edge case: p is longer than s even though both use the same repeated letter.

title: Subarray Sum Equals K
description: You're given an array of numbers (which may include negative numbers) and a target number, k. Count how many continuous chunks of the array add up to exactly k.

examples.explanation: Two overlapping chunks, both containing two 1's, add up to 2.
The chunks [1,2] and [3] both sum to 3.

hints: Keep a running total as you scan the array, and check whether (running total - k) has occurred before.
Store how many times each running total has occurred so far in a HashMap, starting with {0: 1}.
followUp: What if all numbers are positive? Can you use sliding window?

testCases.note: Standard case with overlapping matches.
Two different chunks both reaching the target sum.
Edge case: a single-element array with no chunk summing to zero.
Edge case: negative numbers create multiple chunks that sum to zero.
Edge case: negative numbers involved in the only valid chunk.

title: Daily Temperatures
description: You're given a list of daily temperatures. For each day, figure out how many days you'd have to wait until a warmer day comes along. If no warmer day ever comes, put 0 for that day instead.

examples.explanation: Each value tells you how many days to wait for a strictly warmer day.
Since temperatures keep rising, each day only waits 1 day, except the last which never gets warmer.

hints: Keep a stack of day-indices that are still waiting for a warmer day, in decreasing temperature order.
When a warmer day appears, pop from the stack and calculate the difference in indices as your answer.
followUp: What if temperatures can be negative?

testCases.note: Standard mixed-temperature example.
Edge case: strictly increasing temperatures.
Edge case: strictly decreasing temperatures, so no day ever gets warmer.
Edge case: a single day, with no future day to compare against.
Edge case: all the same temperature, so it never gets strictly warmer.

title: Copy List with Random Pointer
description: You're given a special linked list where every node has a normal 'next' pointer plus an extra 'random' pointer that can point to any other node in the list (or to nothing at all). Create a completely separate deep copy of this list, so that changing the copy never affects the original.

examples.explanation: A fully independent deep copy is created, matching every next and random pointer.
Even when nodes point to each other via random pointers, the copy preserves the same structure.

constraints: Node.random is null or points to some node in the list.
hints: Use a HashMap to map each original node to its newly created copy.
First pass: create all the copy nodes. Second pass: use the HashMap to set each copy's next and random pointers.

youtubeVideos.title: Copy List with Random Pointer - NeetCode

relatedProblems: Clone Binary Tree With Random Pointer
followUp: Can you solve it in O(1) space by interleaving the copy nodes?

testCases.note: Standard multi-node example with various random pointer targets.
Edge case: an empty list, allowed by the constraints.
Edge case: a single node with no random pointer at all.
Edge case: a single node whose random pointer points back to itself.
Edge case: two nodes whose random pointers point to each other.

title: LRU Cache
description: Design a storage system (a 'cache') with a fixed capacity that follows the 'Least Recently Used' (LRU) rule: whenever it's full and a new item needs to be added, it removes whichever item hasn't been used in the longest time. You need two operations: get(key), which returns the stored value (or -1 if the key isn't there), and put(key, value), which adds or updates a key. Both operations must run in constant time.

examples.input: LRUCache(2), put(1,1), put(2,2), get(1), put(3,3), get(2), put(4,4), get(1), get(3), get(4)
examples.explanation: With capacity 2, adding a third key evicts whichever key was least recently used.
With capacity 1, adding a second key immediately evicts the first.

constraints: At most 2 * 10^5 calls to get and put.
hints: Combine a HashMap (for instant key lookup) with a doubly linked list (for instant reordering).
Move a node to the front of the list every time it's accessed via get or put; remove from the back when the cache is full.
followUp: How would you implement LFU cache?

testCases.input: capacity=2, put(1,1), put(2,2), get(1), put(3,3), get(2)
testCases.note: Standard eviction case: 2 gets evicted since it was least recently used.
Edge case: capacity of 1 means the very first key gets evicted immediately.

testCases.input: capacity=2, put(1,1), get(1), put(2,2), put(3,3), get(1)
testCases.note: Edge case: accessing key 1 with get() protects it from eviction.
Edge case: calling get() on a completely empty cache.
Edge case: updating an existing key's value shouldn't trigger any eviction.

title: Minimum Window Substring
description: You're given two strings, s and t. Find the shortest continuous chunk of s that contains every character from t, including matching duplicate counts (so if t needs two 'a's, your chunk needs at least two 'a's too). If no such chunk exists, return an empty string.

examples.explanation: "BANC" is the smallest chunk of s containing an A, a B, and a C.
The entire string is already the smallest valid window.

constraints: s and t consist of uppercase and lowercase English letters.
hints: Use a sliding window paired with two frequency maps: one for what's needed and one for what's currently inside the window.
Only start shrinking the window from the left once every required character has enough copies inside it.
relatedProblems: Substring with Concatenation of All Words
Smallest Range Covering Elements from K Lists
followUp: What if you need all minimum windows (not just one)?

testCases.note: Classic example requiring three different characters.
Edge case: s doesn't contain enough copies of the required character.
Edge case: smallest possible input, s exactly equals t.
Edge case: only one required character out of a longer string.
Edge case: needing two of the same character, using the entire string.

title: First Missing Positive
description: You're given an unsorted array of numbers. Find the smallest positive whole number (1, 2, 3, ...) that is not present anywhere in the array.

examples.explanation: 1 and 2 are both present, so 3 is the smallest missing positive number.
1, 3, and 4 are present, but 2 is missing.

hints: The answer always lies somewhere between 1 and (array length + 1).
Use the array itself as a hash map: try to place each number v at index v-1 by swapping.
Scan afterward for the first index i where nums[i] doesn't equal i+1 — that's your missing number.
relatedProblems: Find All Numbers Disappeared in an Array
followUp: What would change if you could use O(n) extra space?

testCases.note: Standard case, missing number comes right after the present ones.
Negative numbers are present but ignored.
Edge case: every number from 1 up to n is present, so the answer is n+1.
Edge case: no positive numbers exist at all in the array.
Edge case: smallest possible array, with the only positive number already present.

title: LFU Cache
description: Design a cache (a small fast-access storage system) with a fixed capacity that follows the 'Least Frequently Used' (LFU) rule: when it's full and needs to evict something, it removes whichever item has been accessed the fewest number of times. If there's a tie between multiple items with the same low frequency, evict whichever one hasn't been used in the longest time. You need get(key) (returns the value, or -1 if missing) and put(key, value) (inserts or updates), both running in constant time.

examples.input: LFUCache(2), put(1,1), put(2,2), get(1), put(3,3), get(2), get(3), put(4,4), get(1), get(3), get(4)
examples.explanation: Key 2 gets evicted because it was used less frequently than key 1.
With zero capacity, nothing can ever actually be stored.

constraints: At most 2 * 10^5 calls to get and put.
hints: Use three HashMaps together: key-to-value, key-to-frequency, and frequency-to-ordered-set-of-keys.
Keep track of the current minimum frequency across the whole cache to instantly know which group to evict from.
followUp: How does LFU differ from LRU in real cache performance?

testCases.input: capacity=2, put(1,1), put(2,2), get(1), put(3,3), get(2)
testCases.note: Standard case: key 2 is evicted for being used less often than key 1.
Edge case: zero capacity means nothing can ever be stored at all.
Edge case: capacity of 1 forces immediate eviction whenever a new key is added.

testCases.input: capacity=3, put(1,1), put(2,2), put(3,3), get(1), get(1), get(2), put(4,4), get(3)
testCases.note: Edge case: key 3 has the lowest usage frequency, so it gets evicted when the cache is full.
Edge case: updating an existing key's value still counts as using it, and doesn't evict anything.

title: Substring with Concatenation of All Words

Find every starting position in s where a chunk of text is made up of all the words in the list glued together, in any order, using each word exactly once (for example, if words = ['foo','bar'], both 'foobar' and 'barfoo' would count).
